teach.why: Van Gogh painted this night scene of a café terrace in Arles in 1888, working outdoors at night rather than from memory or in a studio. The stars are placed to match the real night sky over Arles in mid-September 1888, and the terrace is lit by gas lamp.

notes.head: Starry sky
notes.body: Look at the thick bursts of yellow, white and pale blue, with halo-like rings around the larger stars. Their positions match the real night sky over Arles in September 1888.

notes.head: Glowing awning
notes.body: The large yellow awning is a flat, bright surface that glows almost as brightly as the café interior. It stands out strongly against the blue sky.

notes.head: Cobblestones
notes.body: The pavement is built from many short curved dark and light strokes, one small arc of paint each.

notes.head: Dark tree
notes.body: A dark green tree at the right edge is the only unlit, organic silhouette, set against the starry sky.

notes.head: Warm light against deep blue
notes.body: The whole image is organized around the warm yellow-orange of the lit café at left set against the deep cobalt blue of the sky and buildings. This contrast pulls your eye to the café first, and the terrace is lit by gas lamp.

notes.head: Stars built from strokes
notes.body: The stars are clusters of short, thick strokes radiating outward, not simple dots, with halo-like rings around the larger ones. Their positions match the sky over Arles on 16 or 17 September 1888.

notes.head: Painted on the spot
notes.body: Van Gogh painted this at night, in situ, rather than from memory or in the studio. Look at the thick bursts of yellow, white and pale blue paint in the sky.

notes.head: Pavement made of marks
notes.body: The cobblestones are made of many short curved dark and light strokes, each a small arc of paint. These marks keep your eye moving across the foreground.

afterTeach.why: Vincent van Gogh painted this café terrace in Arles in 1888, working outdoors at night rather than in a studio. The stars in the painting match the real night sky over Arles on 16 or 17 September 1888, so the sky is a record of a particular night. It is also worth looking at for how it handles colour and brushwork: warm lamplight against deep blue, built from thick, visible strokes.

notes.head: The glowing awning
notes.body: The large yellow awning is a flat, bright surface that glows almost as brightly as the café interior. It stands out against the blue sky and pulls the eye to the lit café.

notes.head: The starry sky
notes.body: Thick bursts of yellow, white and pale blue paint make the stars, with halo-like rings around the larger ones.

notes.head: Cobblestones in arcs
notes.body: Each small curved stroke of dark or light paint forms part of the pavement.

notes.head: Dark tree at the edge
notes.body: A dark green tree at the right edge is the only unlit, organic silhouette, set against the starry sky.

notes.head: Warm light against deep blue
notes.body: The picture is organized around warm yellow-orange on the lit café at left, set against deep cobalt blue in the sky and buildings. This strong contrast draws the eye to the café first, then lets it move out into the dark. The café is lit by gas lamp, not electric light.

notes.head: Stars made of strokes
notes.body: The stars are clusters of short, thick strokes radiating outward, not simple dots. The larger ones have halo-like rings, and the yellow, white and pale blue paint stands out against the dark sky. The positions of these stars match the sky over Arles on 16 or 17 September 1888.

notes.head: A pavement built stroke by stroke
notes.body: The foreground cobblestones are made of many short curved dark and light strokes, each a small arc of paint. Up close the ground reads as a surface of separate marks, so you can see how the paint was applied.

notes.head: Painted on the spot
notes.body: Van Gogh made this oil painting en plein air at night, in situ and not from memory or in the studio. That means the scene of the terrace, sky and houses was worked out in front of the place itself.

guide.a: The painting depicts a café terrace in Arles, in France.
The star positions correspond astronomically to the night sky over Arles on 16 or 17 September 1888.
No. Van Gogh painted it en plein air at night, in situ, not from memory or in the studio.

guide.q: What kind of light is the café using?
guide.a: The terrace is lit by gas lamp, not electric light. The light source inside the café is mostly hidden, while the gold awning carries the glow.

teach.why: Composition VII is an oil painting made by Wassily Kandinsky in Munich in 1913, and it is catalogued as abstract art. Scholars identify themes of the Flood, Last Judgment, and Resurrection as embedded in it, even though the canvas shows no clear narrative subject.

notes.head: Striped ladder-like cluster
notes.body: Left of center, a curved, ladder-like cluster of striped lines carries red, blue and yellow hatching. Its dense stripes stand out from the broader color fields around it and draw the eye.

notes.head: Color set side by side
notes.body: Warm yellows, oranges and reds sit directly beside blues and greens across the whole canvas. The transitions are mostly abrupt, so the contrasts make the eye jump from one patch to the next.

notes.head: Lines over color
notes.body: Thin black strokes overlay broader color fields, mostly in the left-center and center. The fine lines contrast with the wider areas of color and give the eye paths to follow across the middle of the canvas.

notes.head: No clear subject
notes.body: Colored shapes and line accents are spread across the canvas with no clear narrative subject. Scholars nonetheless identify themes of the Flood, Last Judgment, and Resurrection as embedded in the work.

notes.head: Made through many studies
notes.body: Over thirty preliminary studies were created for this painting, in Indian ink, watercolor, diagrams, and on canvas. The finished canvas dates from 1913, during Kandinsky's Munich period.

afterTeach.why: Composition VII is an abstract oil painting that Wassily Kandinsky made in Munich in 1913. Scholars find themes of the Flood, Last Judgment, and Resurrection embedded in it, even though the canvas shows no clear narrative subject.

notes.head: Ladder-like cluster
notes.body: A curved, ladder-like cluster of striped lines with red, blue and yellow hatching sits left of center. Its stripes and curve stand out against the broader color fields around it and draw the eye.

notes.head: Black linear strokes
notes.body: Thin black strokes lie over broader color fields, mostly in the left-center and center. Their darkness contrasts with the color beneath and gives the eye lines to follow.

notes.head: Warm beside cool
notes.body: Yellows, oranges and reds sit right next to blues and greens, with mostly abrupt transitions. The sharp contrast makes each patch of color stand out from its neighbor.

notes.head: Color set side by side
notes.body: Warm yellows, oranges and reds sit directly beside blues and greens across the whole canvas. The transitions are mostly abrupt, so the eye keeps jumping between warm and cool areas instead of settling in one place.

notes.head: Line over color
notes.body: Thin black strokes run over broader fields of color, mostly in the left-center and center. The dark lines contrast with the color beneath them and give the eye paths to follow across the surface.

notes.head: No single subject
notes.body: Colored shapes and line accents are spread across the canvas with no clear narrative subject, which fits its catalog style of abstract art. Scholars nonetheless identify themes of the Flood, Last Judgment, and Resurrection embedded in the painting.

notes.head: Prepared in many studies
notes.body: Over thirty preliminary studies were made for this painting, in Indian ink, watercolor, diagrams, and on canvas. The painting was made in 1913, during Kandinsky's Munich period.

guide.q: Where and when was Composition VII made?
guide.a: It was made in Munich, Germany, in 1913. This was during Kandinsky's Munich period.

guide.q: What is the painting a picture of?
guide.a: It has no clear narrative subject; colored shapes and line accents are spread across the canvas. Scholars identify themes of the Flood, Last Judgment, and Resurrection embedded in it.

guide.q: Was it painted in one go?
guide.a: No. Over thirty preliminary studies were made for it, in Indian ink, watercolor, diagrams, and on canvas.
The painting is in oil paint.

teach.why: Antonio Canova carved this marble group in 1794 in the Neoclassical style, showing Cupid holding Psyche in his arms. It is designed to be seen from multiple viewpoints, so the figures reward a walk around them rather than a single glance. A second version was commissioned by Prince Yusupov in 1796 and is now at the Hermitage Museum, Saint Petersburg.

notes.head: Cupid's wings
notes.body: Two upswept feathered wings rise above Cupid, largely separate from his body. Their upward sweep carries the eye to the top of the group.

notes.head: Drapery around Psyche
notes.body: Look at the fine ridges and deeper folds at the hip and thigh, where shadow lines make the sheet read as cloth.

notes.head: The rock base
notes.body: The rock is rougher and more textured than the polished skin above it.

notes.head: A diagonal that leads the eye
notes.body: The composition rises diagonally from the reclining figure at lower right, through the embrace at center, to the wings at upper left. This line carries your eye across the whole group, and because the work is made to be seen in the round, you can keep following it as you move.

notes.head: Smooth skin against rough rock
notes.body: The figures' skin looks smooth and glossy, while the rock base below is rougher and shows tool marks. That contrast sets the polished figures apart from the base they rest on.

notes.head: Cloth carved in stone
notes.body: Drapery around Psyche's lower body shows thin ridges and folds with fine shadows that read as cloth. The shadow lines in the folds give the marble a soft, fabric-like look.

notes.head: Faces turned toward each other
notes.body: The two faces are turned toward each other in a kiss, and Cupid's eyes look downward. Neither figure looks at the viewer, so your attention stays on the embrace itself.

afterTeach.why: Antonio Canova carved this marble group in 1794 in the Neoclassical style. It shows Cupid holding Psyche, and it is made to be seen from many sides, not just one.

notes.head: Cupid's wings
notes.body: Two upswept feathered wings rise above Cupid, largely separate from his body, with feather tips standing out from the wall. They carry the eye up to the top of the composition.

notes.head: Drapery on Psyche
notes.body: The sheet over Psyche's hip and legs has thin ridges and folds with fine shadows that read as cloth.

notes.head: Polished skin, rough rock
notes.body: Compare the polished skin of the figures with the rougher, textured rock they rest on.

notes.head: A sculpture to walk around
notes.body: This sculpture is designed to be seen from several viewpoints, so one photograph shows only part of it. From the view shown, the composition rises on a diagonal from the reclining figure at lower right, through the embrace, to the wings at upper left, and the eye follows that line upward.

notes.head: Smooth skin against rough rock
notes.body: The figures' skin looks smooth and polished, while the rock base below is rougher and shows tool marks. This contrast in marble surfaces sets the figures apart from the base and draws the eye to them.

notes.head: Wings and cloth in marble
notes.body: Cupid's large wings rise above him, with individual feathers carved. The sheet around Psyche's lower body has thin ridges and deeper folds that cast fine shadow lines, so the stone reads as cloth.

notes.head: Faces turned toward each other
notes.body: The two faces are turned toward each other in a kiss, and Cupid's eyes look downward. Neither figure looks at the viewer, so the eye stays on the embrace.

guide.q: What story does the sculpture show?
guide.a: It is titled Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss. In the myth, Psyche opens a forbidden vessel from the underworld and falls into a deathlike sleep.

guide.q: Is there more than one version?
guide.a: Yes. Prince Yusupov commissioned a second version in 1796, and it is now at the Hermitage Museum in Saint Petersburg.

guide.q: What is it made of, and in what style?
guide.a: It is carved in marble and is in the Neoclassical style.

guide.q: Where and when was it made?
guide.a: It was made in Italy and dates from 1794.

teach.why: This oil painting on canvas is attributed to Caravaggio and dates to the 1590s, in the Baroque style. Caravaggio was employed in d'Arpino's workshop specifically to paint fruit and flowers, and a 2012 technical analysis found an underlying drawing that confirms he worked from direct observation of nature.

notes.head: The young man
notes.body: The brightly lit shoulder and white sleeve stand out from the dark background, so the eye lands on the boy holding the basket first.

notes.head: Bunches of grapes
notes.body: Notice the small highlight on each pale berry. These bright points make the cluster stand out.

notes.head: A drooping autumn leaf
notes.body: A yellow-brown leaf hangs at the lower right, toward the viewer's side, over the rim area of the basket.

notes.head: Peaches and apples
notes.body: Look among the fruit for the peaches and apples. They sit alongside grapes and other fruit in the same basket.

notes.head: A figure lit against darkness
notes.body: The bare shoulder and white sleeve are brightly lit against a dark, mostly plain brown-black background. This contrast sets the figure apart and draws the eye first to the young man holding the basket.

notes.head: A basket full of varied fruit
notes.body: The basket holds peaches, apples, grapes and other fruit, with small red fruit, figs and pomegranate also visible.

notes.head: Highlights on the grapes
notes.body: At the right, pale green-white grapes each carry a small bright highlight. These tiny points of light make the berries look rounded and glossy.

notes.head: Painted from life
notes.body: It confirms Caravaggio worked from direct observation of nature.

afterTeach.why: Boy with a Basket of Fruit is an oil painting attributed to Caravaggio, made in Italy in the late 16th century. Caravaggio was employed in Cavalier d'Arpino's workshop specifically to paint fruit and flowers, and a 2012 technical analysis found a preparatory drawing underneath, which shows he worked from direct observation of nature. A brightly lit figure and a heaped basket of fruit stand out against a dark background.

notes.head: The lit figure
notes.body: A young man holding the basket sits brightly lit against the dark background, with a bare shoulder and white sleeve. The light makes this the first place the eye lands.

notes.head: Grapes with highlights
notes.body: Look at the cluster of pale green-white grapes at the right of the basket, where each berry has a small highlight.

notes.head: The drooping leaf
notes.body: A yellow-brown leaf hangs from a vine at the lower right, over the rim area and toward the viewer's side.

notes.head: Light against dark
notes.body: A brightly lit figure with a bare shoulder and white sleeve sits against a mostly plain brown-black background. The strong contrast sets the figure apart and pulls the eye forward, because the background offers nothing else to look at.

notes.head: A basket full of different fruit
notes.body: The basket holds peaches, small red fruit, several kinds of grape, apples or pears, and other fruit such as figs and a pomegranate.

notes.head: Painted from observation
notes.body: A 2012 technical analysis found a preparatory drawing beneath the paint. This confirms Caravaggio worked from direct observation of nature.

notes.head: Highlights on the grapes
notes.body: The pale grapes at the right each carry a small bright highlight. These small points of light make the berries read as separate, rounded forms.

guide.q: How did the painting come to the Borghese collection?
guide.a: It entered the Borghese collection when papal authorities confiscated Cavalier d'Arpino's paintings in 1607. Pope Paul V then donated it to Cardinal Scipione Borghese.
He was employed in d'Arpino's workshop specifically to paint fruit and flowers.
A 2012 technical analysis revealed a preparatory drawing under the paint. This confirmed he worked from direct observation of nature.

guide.q: Is it certain that Caravaggio painted it?
guide.a: The painting is described as attributed to Caravaggio, and the museum lists him as the artist.
